item.title: d-pod realization of nonadiabatic holonomic quantum computation
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Nonadiabatic holonomic quantum computation generalizes to a d-pod system of d ground states coupled to a single excited state, realizing universal single- and two-qudit gates in the Grassmannian 𝒢(d+1;d). For qutrits (d=3), 𝕏3, ℤ3, and 𝕋3 require two pulses, the entangling controlled-ℤ3 gate requires two pulses, and the Hadamard gate ℍ3 requires at most three pulses.

Grade 0.480 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Oskar Axelsson, Claes Fälth, Elias Henriksson Lindberg, Erik Sjöqvist

Figure

Level schematic of the d-pod qudit system showing d computational ground states coupled to an excited state |e⟩ (left) and the equivalent Morris-Shore basis where only the single bright state |b⟩ couples to |e⟩ (right).

Asks

How can nonadiabatic holonomic quantum computation be systematically generalized from three-level Λ qubit systems to qudit configurations using only a single auxiliary excited state?

Before

Prior nonadiabatic holonomic qudit schemes required multiple auxiliary excited states or dark-path configurations.

But

Rotating wave approximation with resonant monochromatic fields, equal temporal envelopes Ω(t) across couplings, and time-independent coupling parameters during each pulse.

Tools

Grassmannian non-Abelian holonomies · Morris-Shore dark-bright state decomposition · Sørensen-Mølmer conditional ion coupling · Householder transformations

Abstract

Holonomic quantum computation (HQC) realizes quantum gates through non-Abelian geometric phases, providing an experimentally accessible approach to quantum control. While the nonadiabatic HQC framework has been extensively developed for three-level Λ systems encoding qubits, its systematic extension to higher-dimensional qudits remains largely unexplored. In this work, we generalize nonadiabatic HQC to a d-pod configuration, where a single excited state is coupled to d ground states, the latter forming the computational subspace. This scheme enables universal holonomic single- and two-qudit gates using only optical or microwave pulses on trapped atoms or ions, offering an efficient route to implement a discrete universal gate set with minimal pulse coordination. As an explicit example, we analyze in detail the qutrit (d=3) case, demonstrating compact realizations of single- and two-qutrit holonomic gates, each gate requiring at most two loops in the Grassmannian generated by at most three pulses.

item.title: Quantum Simulation of Two-Dimensional Free Dirac Hamiltonian in Multimode Circuit QED
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Implemented a programmable 2+1D free massive Dirac Hamiltonian in multimode circuit QED. Observed rotational Zitterbewegung whose oscillation frequency increases while amplitude decreases with higher effective mass ΔΩ.

Grade 0.463 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Jiwon Kang, Jiuk Lee, Eliya Blumenthal, Shay Hacohen-Gourgy, Eunseong Kim

Figure

Trajectories and time traces of the simulated 2D position quadratures ⟨Xˆ1⟩ and ⟨Xˆ2⟩. Measured data match open-system simulations showing mass-dependent rotational Zitterbewegung loops.

Asks

Can a fully programmable two-dimensional massive Dirac Hamiltonian, with dynamical quantum operators for both momentum components, be simulated in circuit QED?

Before

1D Dirac dynamics and 2D massless Weyl dynamics were demonstrated in trapped ions, while photonic lattices and fixed-coupling superconducting circuits lacked independent dynamical quantum momentum degrees of freedom.

But

Fidelity bounded by transmon charging energy Ec/h=230 MHz limiting drive power, spin-locking decoherence (T2ρ=17 μs), non-RWA terms, and ±5 kHz Rabi calibration uncertainty.

Tools

transmon qubit · multimode 3D flute cavity (TE101 and TE102 modes) · double-sideband microwave driving · characteristic function measurement

Abstract

Two-dimensional massive Dirac systems feature a gapped Dirac-cone dispersion central to a broad range of phenomena in condensed-matter and topological physics. While quantum simulations have demonstrated one-dimensional Dirac dynamics and two-dimensional massless Weyl dynamics, programmable simulation of massive two-dimensional Dirac dynamics remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we realize a programmable two-dimensional free Dirac Hamiltonian in circuit QED, with independently tunable spin-momentum couplings and mass, using a single Rabi-driven qubit coupled to two modes of a multimode cavity. Using this Hamiltonian, we observe rotational Zitterbewegung of a two-dimensional massive Dirac particle and its dependence on the effective mass. Time-dependent master-equation simulations incorporating measured decoherence, corrections beyond the rotating-wave approximation (RWA), and anharmonicity of the transmon reproduce the observed dynamics. Our results establish multimode circuit QED as a compact, programmable platform for higher-dimensional relativistic quantum dynamics and provide a foundation for exploring dynamical and topological phenomena in gapped Dirac systems.

item.title: Quantum Compiler Design for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Presents a full-stack taxonomy organizing fault-tolerant quantum computing compilation into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC optimization, physical-level hardware realization across superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms, and classical real-time decoder runtime integration.

Grade 0.446 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits” · Chenghong Zhu, Jiahan Chen, Keming He, Hongshun Yao, Zhaohui Yang, Jin-Guo Liu, Anbang Wu, Xiaotong Ni, Xingsheng Luan, Zhuo Fu, Shenggen Zheng, Xin Wang

Figure

Full-stack abstraction of QEC-protected quantum computation, illustrating the compilation flow from logical circuit synthesis to physical hardware mapping and the classical decoding feedback loop.

Asks

How should quantum compilers be architected across the entire hardware and software stack to bridge logical fault-tolerant operations, physical syndrome extraction, and real-time classical decoding?

But

Literature survey covering peer-reviewed papers and substantive preprints available through June 2026.

Tools

Lattice surgery and code surgery · Detector error models · Magic-state distillation scheduling · Real-time decoding and frame tracking

Abstract

Scalable quantum computation is expected to rely on fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC), in which quantum error correction (QEC) suppresses physical errors sufficiently to support reliable logical operations. This requires quantum compilation to move beyond general-purpose circuit optimization toward encoding-aware and protocol-structured compilation across the full stack of fault-tolerant quantum computers. Beyond circuit synthesis and hardware mapping, an FTQC compiler must lower algorithm-level operations into the logical gate set supported by the chosen code, coordinate encoded data and ancilla resources, realize logical operations together with repeated syndrome extraction under hardware constraints, and provide the resulting measurement stream to real-time decoding. This survey presents a full-stack view of compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation. We organize existing work into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration. At the logical level, we review surface-code lattice-surgery compilers, beyond-surface-code code-surgery frameworks including emerging qLDPC approaches, and compilation support for non-Clifford operations such as magic-state distillation and code switching. At the physical level, we survey hardware-aware QEC realization on superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms. We further examine decoder models, real-time decoding systems, and frame-management mechanisms that close the feedback loop during fault-tolerant execution. Finally, we identify open challenges in cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and the development of integrated and benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks. An actively maintained paper list is available at: github.com/chenghongz/QEC-compiler-design.

item.title: Indistinguishability of single Raman photons from single atoms
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Mean back-decay count ⟨N⟩ during excitation pulses sets tight upper and lower bounds on Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility VHOM for Raman single photons; for long-distance (>10 km) dual-rail entanglement swapping over standard fiber, 40Ca+ Raman schemes achieve the highest coincidence rates.

Grade 0.442 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Pascal Baumgart, Max Bergerhoff, Jürgen Eschner

Figure

Dual-rail entanglement-swapping coincidence probability versus SMF-28e+ fiber length across nine Raman photon schemes in 40Ca+, 88Sr+, 138Ba+, and 171Yb+, with and without Purcell enhancement.

Asks

How do spontaneous back-decays during few-nanosecond Raman excitation pulses degrade photon indistinguishability, and how can excitation parameters be optimized across different trapped-ion species?

But

Numerical simulations of effective three-level Λ systems; trapped-ion species comparison relies on published single-photon conversion efficiencies and fiber attenuation rates.

Tools

quantum jump decomposition · quantum regression theorem · master equation simulations · optical cavity Purcell enhancement modeling

Abstract

We theoretically investigate the indistinguishability of single photons generated from single trapped ⁴⁰Ca⁺ ions in a Raman scattering process driven by few-nanosecond excitation pulses. Of particular interest is how spontaneous decay back to the initial state affects Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) photon interference. Numerical simulations identify the mean number of back-decays as a measurable quantity that correlates with achievable HOM visibility. Optimization of the excitation pulse with respect to a trade-off between photon yield and indistinguishability is analyzed. Finally, we compare the performance of different trapped-ion species for long-range dual-rail entanglement swapping via HOM photon interference.

item.title: Pump-Free Microwave-Optical Bell Pair Generation for Teleportation-Based Quantum Transduction
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Protocol generates microwave-optical heralded Bell pairs without an optical pump, reaching heralding rates up to 3.71 kHz with 0.97 fidelity in a 87Rb ensemble.

Grade 0.438 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Fangxin Li, Jaesung Heo, Zhaoyou Wang, Benjamin Pingault, Xingyu Gao, Tengyang Ruan, Anjun Chu, David D. Awschalom, Andrew N. Cleland, Andrew P. Higginbotham, Alexander A. High, Liang Jiang

Figure

Heralding rate and Bell-state fidelity plotted against transmon relaxation time T1,t across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated platforms.

Asks

Can microwave-optical Bell pairs be generated for teleportation-based transduction without relying on an optical pump?

But

Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes zero optical pump during generation, trapping fields switched off in ensembles, and transmon relaxation time T1,t=300 µs.

Tools

MO-NODE protocol · cavity QED · three-level transmon · Purcell-enhanced emission · single spins, atomic ensembles, and spin-phonon systems

Abstract

The coherent conversion between microwave and optical photons, known as quantum transduction, is critical for connecting superconducting processors to optical networks. Existing methods are limited by complications associated with optical pumping. We propose a pump-free microwave-optical Bell-pair source for teleportation-based transduction. Using a spin or atomic system resonantly coupled to optical and microwave cavities, the scheme generates loss-robust heralded Bell pairs. Across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated systems, this assembly achieves kilohertz-range heralding rates with high fidelity.

item.title: Two-Dimensional Materials toward CMOS-Compatible Scalable Quantum Hardware
item.description:
Worth a look review — Assesses transferability of CMOS-compatible 2D material fabrication to solid-state quantum processors to reduce structural disorder and improve qubit coherence.

Grade 0.437 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Mara Lieberegts, Ye Wang

Asks

Can 2D material processes developed for next-generation CMOS be adapted to manufacture scalable, high-coherence quantum chips?

But

Perspective and synthesis; qualitative roadmap rather than primary experimental data.

Tools

2D materials · van der Waals heterostructures · CMOS-compatible fabrication · solid-state quantum processors

Abstract

Manufacturability is one of several constraints on developing solid-state quantum processors, along with qubit performance, control, connectivity, cryogenic operation, and fault tolerance. Chemical residues, structural disorder, and non-uniform interfaces introduced during fabrication can compromise qubit coherence. Two-dimensional (2D) materials, with their atomically thin crystals and van der Waals interfaces, offer routes to address some of these challenges. Their concurrent development as next-generation CMOS channel materials motivates an examination of whether relevant processes can be transferred to quantum chips. This Perspective evaluates the opportunities and limitations of 2D materials for CMOS-compatible quantum hardware.

item.title: Pulse-Level Compilation of Measurement-Free Recovery in Transmon Circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Local quantum error correction recovery rules compile into fixed, open-loop microwave pulses on leaf auxiliary transmons via condition-dependent spectral shifts, executing a four-qubit repetition code cycle in 560 ns within a 1 ̀s repetition period.

Grade 0.415 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum memories and repeaters for long-distance links” · Yi-Han Yu, Kai Xu, Heng Fan

Figure

Decay of logical coherence CY under dressed Pauli-X noise (̃_X = (30 μs)⁻¹) and logical-one population P1L under amplitude damping (T1=30μs) versus time over repeated 1 ̀s cycles. The compiled open-loop recovery slows decay compared to uncorrected encoded states and single physical qubits.

Asks

Can joint syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback be compiled into a fixed open-loop control waveform via the conditional energy spectrum of an interacting transmon network?

But

Numerical simulation assuming ideal, instantaneous auxiliary reset and calibrated branch phases; noise during drives is approximated by interleaved channel factors.

Tools

Spectrally selective longitudinal and two-photon transverse drives · Transmon circuit full-Hamiltonian numerics (4 levels per mode) · Pipelined two-color scheduling · SQUID-mediated tunable couplers

Abstract

Quantum error correction commonly relies on syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback. We numerically show that the conditional spectrum of an interacting transmon circuit can compile a local recovery rule into a fixed open-loop control cycle. In a four-bit repetition-code ring, the resulting input-independent control slows the decay of logical coherence under Pauli-\(X\) noise and stabilizes logical-one population under data relaxation relative to uncorrected references. Its local, bounded-degree architecture provides a hardware-native framework for extending compiled recovery control to larger quantum networks.

item.title: Probabilistic Error Cancellation for Single-Mode Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Codes
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) applied over a round of continuous-variable GKP error correction yields quasiprobability sampling overheads Cem for single- and two-qubit logical Clifford gates as a function of finite squeezing parameter ΔdB, evaluated for square and hexagonal GKP codes under Steane and teleportation syndrome extraction.

Grade 0.408 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Victoria Wadewitz, Alessandro Ciani

Figure

Circuit equivalence maps converting hexagonal GKP syndrome extraction circuits into equivalent square GKP code gates and states for teleportation-based and Steane-type continuous-variable error correction protocols.

Asks

How can probabilistic error cancellation be applied together with continuous-variable GKP error-correcting cycles to mitigate residual logical noise from finite squeezing?

But

Noise modeled as isotropic Gaussian random displacement; single round of QEC; finite squeezing treated with twirled/well-characterized approximations without experimental noise learning.

Tools

stabilizer subsystem decomposition · probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) · Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes · Gaussian random displacement channel model · Zak basis

Abstract

In order to solve practical problems on a quantum computer, it is necessary to use fault-tolerant quantum error correction schemes to overcome noise: the errors arising from imperfections in physical components. The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code aims at achieving this in a hardware efficient manner by encoding finite-dimensional logical subspaces in the Hilbert space of one or more continuous variable modes. In near term implementations, however, it is not feasible to eliminate errors entirely, so it is natural to also employ alternative error mitigation techniques together with error correction. In this work, we study a quantum error mitigation method known as probabilistic error cancellation in the context of the GKP code. We compare Steane-type and teleportation-based GKP error correction, and calculate the sampling overheads associated with the technique for square and hexagonal GKP codes. We employ the stabilizer subsystem decomposition for GKP codes to obtain an effective logical channel for noisy operations that is used to express the ideal one of a target logical unitary. We consider noise from finite squeezing on the data and the two ancilla modes, needed for error correction, and examine the relationship between the sampling overhead and the noise for different decoding methods. Our results are calculated for single- and two-qubit GKP Clifford gates and one round of error correction, and show the nontrivial combination of error correction and mitigation in continuous variable codes.
